castling.title: An attacked crossing square
steps: Keep the history and space checks
The king and h1 rook have never moved; the path is empty.
Those conditions pass, but they are only part of the castling test.
The king must be safe on its starting square, crossing square and destination.
F1 is a crossing square. Its being attacked is enough to forbid castling, even if g1 is safe.
An unmoved rook and an empty path do not repair an attacked king route.

castling.title: Returning home does not restore the right
steps: The king went from e1 to e2 earlier.
Castling rights depend on the moves already played, not only the pieces’ current squares.
The king is back on e1; the path is empty and safe.
Those are useful present-position checks, but they do not undo the earlier king move.
The right to castle was lost when the king moved.
A rook staying unmoved does not restore the king’s lost right.
Keep this history check alongside the route and attack checks.

physics-2.title: Find kinetic energy from mass and speed
steps: Mass is 10 kg and speed is 4 m/s. The square belongs to the speed.
Multiplying mass by unsquared speed would be a different calculation.
State the result with its unit
The sled has 80 joules of kinetic energy.
Kilograms times metres squared per second squared gives joules.

corrections.40: A numerical result of 40 comes from 10 × 4, mass times unsquared speed. For kinetic energy, use ½ × 10 × 4² = 80 J.

physics-2.title: Recover speed from kinetic energy
steps: The unknown is speed; write the square explicitly before rearranging.
Multiplying by 2 removes the one-half, then dividing by mass isolates v².
Sixteen is the value of v². Speed is its positive square root.
Putting 4 m/s back into the energy expression recovers the supplied 200 joules.

test-interpretation.title: A positive result when the condition is uncommon
steps: Keep the much larger unaffected group in view.
Sensitivity acts on the group who actually have the condition.
Specificity of 95% leaves a 5% false-positive rate among people without the condition.
Use all positive results as the denominator
About 15% of positive results in this example are true positives. A positive screening result is not itself a diagnosis.

test-interpretation.title: The same true-positive count, a different base rate
steps: Prevalence tells you the two groups before testing.
These are people with the condition whose tests are positive.
A specificity of 90% means 10% of the unaffected group tests positive.
Compare true positives with all positives
Half of the positive results are true positives here. Sensitivity alone is not the probability of having the condition after a positive test.
